passage: The most familiar objection to industrial policy is that governments cannot pick winners. Officials, the objection runs, have neither the information nor the incentives to know which industries will flourish; investors risking their own money are better placed to judge, and when the state substitutes its judgement for theirs it will usually back the wrong horses and keep feeding them long after the race is lost. The objection has history on its side, in the sense that the record of state-backed ventures includes many expensive failures. But it rests on a picture of the problem that deserves closer inspection.

The picture is one in which the menu of possible industries is known and the only question is which item to choose. Investors, in this picture, already know what a country could produce profitably, and the government's error is to overrule them. Yet for an economy trying to move into activities it has never undertaken, no one possesses this knowledge. Whether a particular region can grow cut flowers for export, assemble electronic components or write software for foreign clients depends on a mass of local particulars, from the reliability of the roads to the habits of the workforce, that can be learned only by trying. An investor asked in advance would have no better basis for a forecast than an official; both would be guessing. The relevant knowledge is not hidden in investors' heads waiting to be consulted; it does not yet exist.

Producing it is costly, and here the market's usual advantages turn against it. The first entrepreneur to discover that a product can be made profitably in a given place bears the full cost of the experiment if it fails, but if it succeeds, others can copy the discovery cheaply, entering the industry once its viability has been shown. The pioneer thus bears the losses of failure while sharing the rewards of success, and rational investors will undertake fewer such experiments than the economy as a whole would want. The case for public involvement follows not from officials knowing more than investors, but from no one knowing enough and the cost of finding out being borne unevenly.

If this is right, the objection about picking winners is aimed at the wrong target. A policy of supporting discovery will back many ventures that fail; that is what experiment means, and a programme that never failed would be one that was taking no risks. Measured by the share of its bets that pay off, a sound programme of discovery may look worse than a timid one. The genuine danger lies elsewhere: support, once given, may become impossible to withdraw, so that the losers are kept alive at public expense. What matters is less the ability to pick winners than the ability to let losers go, and the second ability, though rarely discussed, is at least as hard to acquire as the first.

The approach has a cost of its own, and it would be dishonest to minimise it. Discovering what local firms could do requires officials to work closely with them, to learn what obstacles they face and what help would remove them. The same closeness that yields information also invites capture, in which those meant to be overseen come to set the terms. Officials who meet the same managers every month will find it hard to tell them, when a review date arrives, that support is ending. There is no formula that separates collaboration from collusion, only practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that make the difference easier to see. That is a weaker guarantee than the advocates of industrial policy would like, but it is a stronger one than its critics usually assume.

options.A: A large share of the ventures that governments have backed in the past failed at considerable cost to public funds.
options.B: Later entrants to new export activities usually must repeat nearly all of the pioneer's costly trials, since its lessons cannot be copied.
options.C: Officials frequently lack detailed information about local conditions that the firms operating there already possess.
options.D: Pioneers whose ventures failed had, on average, less access to bank credit than pioneers whose ventures went on to succeed.

passage: Egalitarians hold that there is something wrong with inequality as such: that when some people are much worse off than others through no fault of their own, the situation is bad, and bad in part simply because of the gap. The most famous objection to this view asks us to consider what follows from it. Suppose that the only way to remove an inequality were to make the better off worse off, with no benefit to anyone, as if a town in which some households had gardens and others had none could reach equality only by paving over every garden. If inequality is bad in itself, then such a change would remove something bad, and so would be in one respect an improvement. Yet the change helps no one and harms many. To call it an improvement in any respect, the objectors say, is absurd.

Many philosophers have been moved by this objection to give up equality as a fundamental value. Some have adopted the view that benefits matter more the worse off their recipient is, so that a gain to a poor person counts for more than the same gain to a rich one; others hold that what matters is that everyone should have enough, after which differences cease to be of moral concern. Neither view is troubled by levelling down, since on neither does reducing the well-being of the better off, by itself, improve anything. Both also capture much of what drew people to equality in the first place, which was a concern for those who are badly off.

Yet the objection is less decisive than it is usually taken to be. The egalitarian need not claim that a levelled-down world is better all things considered, only that it is better in one respect while much worse in others. Plural values often pull apart in this way. We can think that a promise kept at terrible cost was in one respect admirable without thinking that it should have been kept. Seen this way, the levelling-down case shows only that equality is not the only thing that matters, which almost no egalitarian ever believed.

This defence succeeds, but at a price. It keeps equality as a value only by making it a strangely impersonal one: something that can make a state of affairs better while making it better for no one at all. Many will find such a value hard to care about. There is, however, another way to understand what egalitarians were after. On a relational view, the core of equality lies not in how goods are distributed but in how people stand to one another: in the absence of rank, servility and contempt, in a society where no one must bow and no one may command another merely by virtue of birth or wealth. Inequalities of resources matter on this view chiefly because, beyond some point, they turn into inequalities of standing, as when wealth buys influence over others or poverty forces deference to them.

The relational view is untouched by the levelling-down objection, because paving over gardens neither creates nor abolishes any relation of rank between neighbours. Whether it can say enough about distribution is a further question. A society might abolish titles and deference while leaving vast differences in income intact, and the relational egalitarian owes us an account of when such differences begin to corrode equal standing. But the view has at least located the value of equality in a relation between persons, which is where most of its defenders always felt it to be.

options.B: could make a situation better even though the situation was better for no particular person.
options.C: applies to the design of public institutions rather than to private relationships between individuals.
options.D: can be assessed only by impartial officials who have no personal stake in how goods are distributed.

passage: Few historical lessons are repeated as confidently as the one drawn from the settlement that followed the First World War. A harsh peace, the lesson runs, breeds resentment, and resentment breeds the next war; a generous peace, by contrast, turns yesterday's enemy into tomorrow's partner. The lesson is attractive because it joins morality to prudence. It tells victors that magnanimity is not only noble but wise, and that they can secure the future simply by being kind. It also offers a single, memorable explanation for one of the great catastrophes of the last century, and explanations of that kind are hard to dislodge once they have settled into textbooks and speeches.

The trouble is that the record does not sort so neatly. Some severe settlements have held for generations, because the defeated party was too weak to overturn them and the victors remained willing to enforce their terms. Some lenient ones have failed, because the loser read leniency as a sign that it had not really been beaten and that a second attempt might succeed. What such cases suggest is that severity and generosity are the wrong variables to watch. A settlement lasts when its terms match the actual balance of strength, and when the powers that wrote it remain prepared to uphold it.

By this measure, the worst settlement is not the harshest but the one that combines harsh terms with a weak will to enforce them. Such a peace gives the defeated every reason to resent the order and no reason to fear challenging it. Its demands are heavy enough to humiliate, yet the victors, tired of war and divided among themselves, let them be evaded piece by piece, until the settlement has lost both its authority and its power to deter. Much of the interwar story can be told in this way, as a failure less of severity than of follow-through.

This is not an argument for cruelty dressed up as realism. Generosity has a real role, but it works best after the defeat has been made unmistakable, when it can be read as the confidence of a winner rather than the hesitation of a power unsure of its victory. Offering a defeated state a path back into the community of nations, through trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions, gives it a stake in the order that no amount of punishment can create. The point is only that kindness must rest on a settlement that is clear about who won and is backed by someone willing to say so.

options.A: A lenient settlement lasted for several decades after the victors made it clear that they had won decisively and would defend its terms.
options.B: A harsh settlement that the exhausted victors stopped enforcing was overturned by the defeated state within a decade of being signed.
options.C: Historians continue to disagree about whether the settlement that followed the First World War was in fact unusually harsh.
options.D: A settlement that matched the balance of strength and was firmly upheld by united victors still collapsed within a few years because its harshness was resented.

passage: When two experts disagree about a question the rest of us cannot assess, it can seem that the layperson has only two options: to become an expert herself, or to pick a side at random. Neither is attractive. The first is usually impossible within the time available, and the second makes a mockery of the idea that belief should answer to evidence. But the dilemma is false. Although the layperson cannot judge the dispute directly, she can often judge the disputants, and judgements of that kind can be reasonable even when the subject matter remains opaque to her.

Several kinds of evidence are available. She can ask whether either expert has a record of predictions that can be checked, and how those predictions fared. She can ask whether one of them stands to gain from being believed, through money, reputation or loyalty to an institution. She can ask how the rest of the field divides, bearing in mind that a majority counts for more when its members reached their views independently than when they all learned them from the same teacher. None of these questions requires understanding the dispute itself. Each concerns the circumstances in which a claim is advanced rather than its technical content, and each can be answered, at least roughly, by an attentive citizen with no specialised training whatever.

One tempting source of evidence is less useful than it looks. Laypeople often favour the expert who argues more fluently, answers objections more quickly and seems more at ease. Yet these are skills of performance, and they are only loosely connected with being right. A careful scientist may hedge, pause and admit uncertainties that a confident charlatan would brush aside, and an audience that rewards confidence is, in effect, rewarding the very habit that should make it suspicious. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that public debate, with its brief exchanges and its appetite for memorable phrases, is arranged almost entirely so as to display performance, and so to favour the disputant who has mastered it.

It would be a mistake to conclude that the layperson's position is comfortable. Track records are often unavailable for the questions that matter most, interests can be hidden, and a field can be captured by a fashion that makes its consensus less independent than it appears. The indirect methods narrow the range of reasonable belief; they rarely close it. Still, a choice made on such grounds is not a coin toss, and treating it as one hands an advantage to whoever is most willing to exploit the public's sense of helplessness.

options.B: can make some lay beliefs about an expert dispute more reasonable than others without guaranteeing a correct choice.
options.C: are of no use when the question in dispute is among the questions that matter most to the public.
options.D: are most useful to a layperson who can also follow the technical arguments that each expert puts forward.

passage: Imagine a small-town bank that is entirely sound: its loans are prudent and its borrowers will repay, although those loans run for years while its deposits can be withdrawn on any day. Suppose a rumour spreads that this institution is in trouble. Each depositor now faces a simple calculation: if others withdraw and I do not, my bank may have to sell its loans in a hurry and at a loss, leaving me with little, whereas if I withdraw first, I lose nothing. It is therefore rational to run whether or not the rumour is true, and once enough people run, the rumour becomes true. Such a bank fails not because it was unsound but because it was believed to be.

Deposit insurance is the classic answer, because a guarantee from the state, up to some limit, alters the calculation entirely. A depositor who stays put loses nothing even if her bank collapses, so she has no reason to join a run, and because no one runs, the guarantee is seldom called upon. Seen in this light, insurance looks almost like a free lunch: a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary.

The objection is familiar. Insured depositors have no reason to ask what their bank does with their money, and a bank whose depositors do not ask can take risks that it would otherwise have to justify to them. The guarantee that ends panics may thus encourage the very recklessness that makes failures likely. Critics conclude that deposit insurance trades a visible problem for a hidden one, and some would scale it back so that depositors once again have a reason to pay attention.

The objection is sound as far as it goes, but it rests on a curious picture of who disciplined banks before guarantees existed. Ordinary depositors were never skilled readers of loan books; what they were skilled at was panic. The discipline they supplied was indiscriminate, striking prudent and imprudent banks without distinction once fear took hold, as the town bank illustrates. If insured depositors stop watching, little genuine scrutiny is lost, and the task passes to those equipped for it: supervisors with the power to inspect, and the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake. The lesson of the objection is not that guarantees are a mistake but that they must be paired with oversight, and that the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care.

options.A: depositors acting sensibly on a rumour bring about the very trouble that the rumour had wrongly alleged.
options.B: the state has not guaranteed its deposits, and so its managers are free to take excessive risks with them.
options.C: its depositors behave irrationally, withdrawing money out of fear when they have no reason to do so.
options.D: its loans turn out to be less prudent than its managers had believed when they first approved them.

passage: The defence of meritocracy rests on a simple and appealing idea: that positions and rewards should go to those who earn them, through talent and effort, rather than to those born into the right family. Against the background of aristocratic privilege this was a revolutionary thought, and it remains a powerful one. Yet it has been attacked, with increasing force, on the ground that talent and effort are themselves largely matters of luck. No one chooses the abilities they are born with. And the capacity to work hard, to persist through failure and to defer gratification, is shaped by upbringing, health and circumstance in ways that no one controls. If this is so, the critic concludes, nobody deserves the rewards that meritocracy hands out, and the language of merit is a flattering fiction.

The premises of this argument are difficult to deny, but its conclusion moves too fast. It runs together two different claims that a person might make about a reward. One is that she deserves it in a deep moral sense, that the world would be unjust if she did not have it. The other is that she is entitled to it, because she has met the conditions that a fair set of rules laid down in advance. A runner who wins a race under fair conditions is entitled to the prize even if her speed owes much to her genes and her coaching; to take the prize away on the ground that she was lucky would itself be a wrong, because she trained and competed on the understanding that winning would bring it. Entitlement of this kind does not depend on the winner being the author of her own talents. It depends only on the fairness of the rules and her compliance with them.

Seen in this light, a society can reward productive contributions, and honour the expectations its rules create, without pretending that the rewards measure the moral worth of those who receive them. It also leaves open, as it should, the question of whether the rules themselves are fair, including how much inequality of reward they ought to permit. What the luck argument undermines is not the practice of rewarding achievement but a particular story told about it, the story in which the successful have simply earned their place and the unsuccessful have simply failed to earn theirs. That story is corrosive. It encourages the winners to regard their advantages as wholly their own, and it adds to the losers' material disadvantage the further injury of being told that they deserved it. The remedy is not to abolish merit but to hold it more lightly.

options.A: A worker paid less than a colleague for the same work complains that the firm's pay scale is unfair to her.
options.B: A firm abolishes all bonuses because its managers conclude that performance is mostly a matter of good luck.
options.C: A runner who finished second insists that she deserved the prize more than the winner because she trained harder.
options.D: A lottery winner has a valid claim to the jackpot under the rules of the draw, though nobody thinks she earned it.

passage: Students and teachers share a reasonable-sounding rule: if learning feels smooth, it is going well. A chapter reread the night before an examination seems familiar, a set of problems practised one type at a time feels increasingly easy, and the growing ease is taken as proof of mastery. The rule is reasonable because in many activities fluency really does track competence. A pianist who plays a passage without stumbling has, in some sense, learned it. Yet in the specific matter of building knowledge that lasts and transfers, the rule is frequently misleading, and sometimes backwards.

The reason is that the conditions which make performance easy during study are often not the conditions which make memory durable. Rereading produces familiarity, the sense of having seen something before, which is easily mistaken for the ability to recall it unaided. Practising one kind of problem in a block lets the learner apply the same procedure again and again without ever deciding which procedure the problem calls for, the very decision a mixed examination demands. By contrast, spacing study sessions apart, testing oneself instead of rereading, and mixing problem types all make study feel slower and more error-prone, and all tend to produce better retention weeks later. The effort of retrieving a half-forgotten fact, or of working out which method applies, appears to be part of what fixes it in memory.

It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this, namely that harder is always better. It is not. A difficulty helps only when the learner can, with effort, overcome it; material pitched far beyond a student's grasp produces confusion rather than consolidation, and a test on something never learned teaches little except discouragement. The useful difficulties are those that call on processes the learner will later need, such as retrieval, discrimination and reconstruction, rather than obstacles that merely slow things down. Printing a textbook in a faint, awkward typeface makes reading harder, but there is little reason to expect it to make anything stick.

The deeper problem is one of judgement. Because learners rely on how study feels, they systematically prefer the methods that serve them worst, and they are not foolish to do so: the costs of effortful methods are felt now, while their benefits arrive later and unannounced. Teachers face a similar temptation, since a lesson in which students struggle looks, to an observer and to the students themselves, like a lesson that has gone badly. Changing practice therefore requires more than information about which methods work. It requires a willingness to distrust a feeling that is usually reliable, in exactly the setting where it is not.

options.A: an unhelpful difficulty, since there is nothing learned for the effort of retrieval to consolidate.
options.B: a useful difficulty, because any effortful test is preferable to the familiarity produced by rereading.
options.C: no less valuable than spacing study sessions apart, provided that the quiz is followed by careful rereading.
options.D: useful chiefly because it shows students how much of the topic still remains for them to learn later.

passage: When a global fast-food chain enters a new country, the first thing commentators examine is its menu. If the chain serves the same burger it serves at home, critics see cultural flattening, the erosion of local tastes by a single corporate palate. If it introduces a spiced vegetable patty or a rice dish for the local market, its defenders announce that globalisation, far from erasing difference, accommodates it. Both sides agree, without ever saying so, that the menu is where the question of cultural influence will be settled.

That assumption deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. A menu is the part of a chain that is easiest to change and, for that very reason, the part that tells us least. What the chain actually exports is a format: a way of organising food, labour and time. The counter at which one orders without a waiter, the fixed price displayed in advance, the promise that the meal will taste the same today as it did last month, the kitchen run like an assembly line by staff who can be trained in days: these travel intact, and they carry assumptions about efficiency and predictability that are far more foreign to many food cultures than any particular ingredient. A spiced patty served through such a system is a local flavour in a global grammar.

Yet it would be wrong to infer that the format simply imposes its meanings wherever it goes, for customers bring meanings of their own. In some places a visit to a chain restaurant has been, at least for a time, a special occasion rather than a convenience: a clean, cool and respectable room in which a family can celebrate a birthday, or two young people can meet without attracting comment. The format was designed for speed, but the customers linger. They take a system built to minimise the time spent at the table and turn it into a place for spending time.

The interesting story, then, has three layers rather than one. The format is global and changes slowly; the meanings attached to it are local and can diverge sharply from what its designers intended; the menu sits between them, adjusted constantly in response to both. To read cultural influence from the menu alone is like judging the spread of a language by the loanwords it has picked up, while ignoring both its grammar and the uses to which its new speakers put it.

options.A: The chain adds several new regional dishes to its menu each year in response to suggestions made by its local customers and staff.
options.B: Families in the country choose the chain's restaurants for birthdays and linger there long after they have finished eating.
options.C: Local family eateries begin taking orders at a counter, posting fixed prices and standardising their kitchens, while still serving their old dishes.
options.D: The chain's outlets in the country sell more of its standard home burger than of the dishes it has created for the local market, year after year.

passage: A familiar picture of scientific objectivity confines values to the edges of inquiry. Values may legitimately decide which problems are worth studying and how results are used, but in the central act of science, deciding whether the evidence supports a hypothesis, they are supposed to have no place. A researcher who lets personal hopes affect whether a conclusion is accepted is, on this picture, simply doing bad science, and the remedy is a stricter separation between the laboratory and the world outside it.

The trouble is that evidence rarely settles a question outright, and so accepting a hypothesis always involves deciding that the evidence is strong enough. How strong is strong enough? Consider a laboratory testing whether an industrial solvent damages the liver. If it wrongly concludes that the solvent is safe, workers may be harmed; if it wrongly concludes that the solvent is dangerous, a useful product may be withdrawn and money wasted. Which error is worse, and therefore how much evidence to demand before declaring the solvent harmful, is not something the data can decide. It depends on how one weighs injured workers against lost revenue, which is a question of value. Two laboratories examining identical data could therefore set the threshold in different places, and neither would have misread a single measurement.

A natural reply is that scientists need not accept or reject anything. They could report the probability that the hypothesis is true, given the evidence, and leave the decision to those who must act. The reply is attractive but harder to carry out than it sounds. Before any probability can be reported, the investigators must decide how to classify ambiguous tissue samples, which measurements to discard as faulty and which statistical model to fit, and each of these decisions can err in either direction, with the same uneven consequences. The weighing of errors does not disappear; it moves to a stage where it is less visible.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that anything goes. The argument shows that values can properly bear on how much evidence to require, given what is at stake if one is wrong. It does not show that values can bear on what the evidence is, or license a researcher to discount an inconvenient result because it is unwelcome. The distinction is between setting the bar and moving the evidence, and the integrity of science depends on keeping the two apart, not on pretending that the bar sets itself.

options.A: transferring the weighing of errors to an earlier stage of the research where it is harder to see.
options.B: raising or lowering the amount of evidence required in the light of what is at stake if one errs.
options.C: allowing a preference for one conclusion to alter what the results are taken to be, for instance by setting aside an unwelcome finding.
options.D: presenting the evidence to the people who must act instead of accepting or rejecting the hypothesis oneself.

passage: Talk of moral progress makes many people uneasy. It sounds like the self-congratulation of every age that has looked back on its predecessors and found them wanting, and it seems to require a fixed standard against which the direction of change could be measured, a standard that is itself in dispute. Yet it is hard to describe the abolition of legal slavery, or the end of public torture as a form of entertainment, merely as changes in fashion, as though they were on a par with a shift in the length of coats. Most people who doubt the idea of moral progress in theory find themselves unable to give it up in particular cases.

One influential way of making sense of the idea is to describe progress as the expansion of a circle of concern. Early moral codes, on this telling, extended full consideration only to kin or to members of the tribe; over time the boundary has been pushed outward, to strangers, to foreigners, to people of other races and faiths, and, more recently and more contentiously, to animals. Progress consists in recognising as morally considerable those whom we previously ignored. The picture is appealing because it gives progress a direction without requiring agreement on a complete moral theory: one needs only the modest premise that arbitrary exclusion is a mistake. It also explains why reformers have so often described their work as opening the eyes of their contemporaries rather than changing their values: the values, on this telling, were already present, and only their application had been blocked.

The picture is not wrong, but it is incomplete in a way that matters. Some of the clearest cases of progress involve not who counts but what we owe to those who already counted. The view that a husband may beat his wife was not, in most societies that held it, a view that wives fell outside moral concern; wives were very much inside the circle, assigned a place in it that we now regard as degrading. Reform came not from widening the boundary but from revising the terms within it. The same is true of changing attitudes to children, who have always been objects of intense concern, and whose treatment has nonetheless been transformed.

There is also a danger in the circle image that its admirers tend to overlook. If progress is measured by the width of the circle, then any extension looks like an advance, and any contraction like a regression. But concern can be extended in ways that are themselves harmful: the circle of a missionary empire was wide, and that width was part of its justification for interfering in other people's lives. Inclusion that comes with a presumption of authority over the included is not obviously better than the indifference it replaces. What matters is not only that more beings are counted, but how they are counted.

None of this means that we should abandon the idea of moral progress. It means that progress is less like a single line along which societies advance and more like a series of corrections, each prompted by the discovery that some practice depended on a mistaken belief, an unexamined interest or a failure of imagination. Such corrections can be recognised as improvements without a finished theory of the good, in the way that a scientist can recognise an error without possessing the final truth. That is a more modest claim than the circle image offers, but it is also harder to dismiss as the vanity of the present.

options.A: Moral progress is real but is better understood as a series of corrections than as the widening of a circle of concern.
options.B: Moral progress is best pictured as a single line along which every society advances in the same direction.
options.C: Talk of moral progress is largely the self-congratulation of each age as it looks back on the ages before it.
options.D: Moral progress consists in extending moral concern to those beings who were previously left outside its boundary.

passage: Few words are used more freely by restaurant reviewers than 'authentic', and few are applied more selectively. A dish is praised as authentic when it is served in a cramped room, by a cook who speaks the diner's language haltingly, at a price that suggests nobody is getting rich. The same dish, served with tablecloths and a wine list, is suspected of having been tamed. Authenticity, in this usage, is less a property of the food than of the scene around it, and the scene is one that the visiting diner has come to consume.

Consider a hypothetical family that opens a restaurant serving the cooking of its home region in a city several thousand kilometres away. From the start, the cooks make changes. Some ingredients cannot be found and are replaced with local ones; some dishes are too laborious for a kitchen that must turn out fifty plates a night; others are sweetened or softened because the first customers sent them back. Within a generation the menu has become something that exists nowhere else: neither the food of the home region nor the food of the new city, but the food of the people who moved between them.

Purists treat this history as a decline, and they reward the restaurants that seem to have resisted it, the ones with a second menu in the home language that outsiders must know to ask for. Yet even that second menu has passed through the same kitchen, the same suppliers and the same compromises. To call it the real food and the first menu a betrayal is to take one stage of a continuous adaptation and freeze it as the original. More troubling, the judgement is usually made by people with no stake in the tradition, who are in effect asking immigrant cooks to perform their own foreignness for an audience's satisfaction.

None of this means that every adaptation is innocent. Cooks under commercial pressure sometimes strip a cuisine of everything difficult until it is recognisable only by name, and something real is lost when that happens. But the loss is better described as a narrowing of what the cooks themselves are free to make than as a departure from a fixed original. The more useful question to ask of a restaurant is not whether its food matches some imagined source, but whether the people cooking it have the room to cook what they think is good.

options.A: The dishes on such second menus are found to be prepared with imported ingredients and unchanged methods, and to match versions cooked in the home region.
options.B: Reviewers praise restaurants with second menus more highly than restaurants that offer only a single menu to all diners, whatever the cooking on either menu is like.
options.C: Many cooks who run such restaurants say they would like to cook more ambitious dishes than their customers will accept, and would do so if the rent allowed it.
options.D: Diners from the home community order mostly from the second menu, while other customers rarely know that it exists or how to ask for it.

passage: Economists who agree that carbon emissions should carry a price often disagree, sometimes heatedly, about how the price should be set. One camp prefers a tax: the government announces a charge per tonne of emissions and leaves firms to decide how much to cut. The other prefers a cap with tradable permits: the government fixes the total quantity of emissions allowed, issues permits for that amount, and lets trading among firms determine what a permit costs. In a world without uncertainty the two would be equivalent. Any cap implies some price at which permits would trade, and any tax implies some level to which emissions would fall; a regulator who knew the costs of abatement could reach the same outcome by either route.

The difference appears once we admit that no one knows those costs in advance. A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned. A cap fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain: if cutting proves harder, permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply. Which uncertainty is more tolerable depends on the shape of the damage. If each additional tonne does roughly the same harm as the last, a fixed price tracks the damage well and a volatile price merely adds cost. If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price. Because the harm from carbon depends on the stock accumulated in the atmosphere over decades rather than on any single year's emissions, many economists conclude that year-to-year overshoots matter little and that a tax, or something that behaves like one, is the better instrument.

Advocates of trading reply that this argument, persuasive in the seminar room, neglects politics. A cap states its environmental goal openly, which can make it easier to defend, and the free allocation of permits to affected industries, though it hands them a windfall, has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted at all. A tax, by contrast, announces a cost to every voter and invites a fresh campaign against it with every scheduled rise.

The more telling fact is that, in practice, the two designs have drifted towards each other. Trading schemes have acquired price floors, to keep permits from becoming nearly worthless when demand falls, and price ceilings, to stop them from spiking; taxes have been given scheduled increases linked to emissions targets. The resulting hybrids are neither pure price nor pure quantity. This convergence suggests that the long debate was, in part, a debate about labels. What decides whether a carbon price works is less whether it is called a tax or a cap than whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough that firms invest on the expectation that it will last.

options.A: a limit on discharges paired with a ceiling on the permit price, since that keeps costs predictable if cutting proves hard.
options.B: a limit on the total quantity discharged, since keeping below the threshold matters more than a predictable cost.
options.C: a fixed charge per unit discharged, since the harm depends on what accumulates over decades and not on any one season.
options.D: either instrument equally well, since a regulator who chose the right level could reach the same outcome by both.

passage: In a handful of democracies, adults who fail to vote without a good excuse are fined a small sum. To many people elsewhere this looks like a contradiction in terms: surely a free citizen is entitled to stay at home. The objection deserves a hearing, but it is less forceful than it first appears. What such laws typically require is attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular. Ballots remain secret, and a citizen who wishes to register indifference or protest can spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank. The duty imposed is closer to that of serving on a jury or completing a census form than to an order about what to believe. A subtler version of the objection holds that deliberate abstention is itself a political statement, a refusal to lend legitimacy to a contest one regards as empty. Yet a citizen who feels this way loses very little under compulsion, since the blank ballot preserves the statement and arguably sharpens it: a deliberately empty ballot can be counted, whereas a deliberate absence is indistinguishable from the absences of those who merely forgot.

The more interesting question is what compulsion actually changes. Where voting is voluntary, turnout is usually lowest among the young, the poor and the recently arrived, so the electorate that politicians court is older and wealthier than the population as a whole. Campaigns respond rationally to this. A large share of their effort goes into persuading their own likely supporters to turn up, and one of the cheapest ways to do that is to make those supporters angry or afraid about the other side. When almost everyone votes, that strategy loses much of its point. There is little to be gained by stirring up people who will vote anyway, and the votes worth competing for belong to citizens who have not yet made up their minds.

Supporters of compulsion sometimes go further and claim that it produces wiser decisions. Here caution is needed. Being required to attend a polling station does not make anyone better informed, and a citizen who resents the obligation may simply mark the first name on the list. Compulsion enlarges the electorate; it does not educate it. Its real contribution is quieter. It shifts the incentives of those who seek votes, away from rousing the faithful and towards addressing the undecided, and it allows the result to claim to speak for nearly everyone rather than for those who happened to feel strongly enough to come out. That is a modest achievement, but in an age of angry campaigning it is not a small one.

options.A: voters who are older and wealthier are, by temperament, more easily made angry or afraid than other citizens.
options.B: getting likely supporters to the polls matters more than winning over the uncommitted, and anger is a cheap way to do it.
options.C: angry voters pay closer attention to policy, and so are more likely to reward a party that offers a well-argued programme.
options.D: undecided citizens can be won over only by campaigns that frighten them about what the other side would do in office.

passage: Modern moral intuition tends to reserve its highest praise for the gift that expects nothing in return. A present given with an eye to what will come back seems to us slightly tarnished, closer to a trade dressed up in ribbon than to generosity. Anthropologists who have studied exchange in a wide range of societies have long found this intuition puzzling, not because people elsewhere are more calculating, but because in most places the obligation to return is understood as part of what a gift is. To receive is to accept a tie; to fail to reciprocate is not merely rude but a refusal of the relationship the gift proposed.

Consider how carefully the timing and size of a return are managed in many communities. A neighbour who sends back a dish of sweets on the very evening she received one has not discharged a debt so much as declined a friendship; the speed of her reply announces that she wants the account closed. A return that matches the original exactly carries a similar message. What sustains the bond is a return that comes later and differs slightly in value, so that one party is always, for the moment, a little in the other's debt. On this view the imbalance is not a flaw to be corrected but the mechanism by which the relationship is kept running: an account that is never quite settled is an account that remains open.

Seen in this light, the free gift is less an ideal than an anomaly. A gift that truly demanded nothing would create no tie, and a society composed only of such gifts would be a collection of strangers who happened to hand each other things. It is telling that the gifts we most often describe as free, such as anonymous donations, are precisely those designed to prevent any relationship between giver and receiver from forming.

None of this means that the obligation to return is always benign. Where one party can give far more than the other could ever repay, the gift becomes an instrument of domination: the receiver is bound by a debt that cannot be cleared, and gratitude hardens into dependence. Patrons have long understood this, and so have recipients of charity, who sometimes refuse help precisely because they cannot answer it. The lesson, however, is not that we should aspire to gifts without strings. It is that the strings must be ones the receiver is able to hold. A generous act, properly understood, is calibrated to the other person's capacity to reply.

options.A: it keeps the poorer neighbour always somewhat in the household's debt, an imbalance that harms the bond in itself.
options.B: any gift given in the expectation of a return is tainted and falls short of real generosity.
options.C: it leaves the neighbour under an obligation he has no way of discharging, so that his thanks become reliance.
options.D: the gifts close the account between the two households before a friendship can develop.

passage: For much of its short history as a subject of research, the wandering mind was treated as noise. Participants in experiments were supposed to attend to the task in front of them, and the moments when their thoughts drifted to lunch or to an argument with a sibling were lapses to be minimised or averaged away. When researchers began to study these lapses directly, by interrupting people at random moments in their day and asking what they had been thinking about, the first surprise was how common the lapses were. The method had the merit of catching thought in the act, before the thinker had time to tidy it into a more respectable account of where her attention had been. A considerable part of waking thought, it turned out, is about something other than what the thinker is doing.

Two quite different interpretations of this finding have since competed. On the first, mind wandering is a failure of control: it is associated with errors in reading and driving, with poorer performance on tests of sustained attention and, in some studies, with lower reported mood at the moment of wandering. The mind that drifts is the mind that has lost its grip, and the remedy is training in attention. On the second interpretation, these costs are real but partial, and they ignore what the drifting mind is actually doing. Much wandering thought is directed at the future, at plans, rehearsals of conversations and the weighing of unfinished business, and some of the solutions that arrive unbidden in the shower or on a walk may owe something to the same process. On this view the mind that drifts is not idle but working on a different problem, one it has judged, so to speak, more pressing than the task at hand.

Each interpretation, I think, makes the same mistake, which is to speak of mind wandering as though it were one thing with one value. The evidence for costs comes largely from tasks that demand continuous attention, where any lapse is damaging by design, while the evidence for benefits comes largely from situations in which the external task is undemanding, so that little is lost by leaving it. Tasks of the first kind are chosen precisely because they make lapses easy to count, and situations of the second kind because they leave room for thought. It is hardly surprising that the two literatures reach different verdicts, since they are, for the most part, looking at different occasions. Nor does the link with low mood settle the matter. A person who is worried is likely both to feel worse and to find his thoughts pulled towards his worries, so that wandering may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause.

A more useful question is not whether the mind should wander but when, and with what awareness. Drifting during a lecture one has chosen to attend is a cost; drifting while washing dishes may be a free opportunity to think. There also seems to be a real difference between thought that slips away unnoticed and thought that is allowed to roam, as when a person deliberately sets a problem aside and lets her attention go where it will. The second kind is under a loose but genuine control, since the person can notice it and call it back. If this is right, the goal of training attention should not be to abolish wandering, an aim that is probably unachievable and possibly harmful, but to make wandering more visible to the wanderer, so that she can tell which kind of occasion she is in.

options.A: Training in attention should be abandoned, since every attempt to suppress the wandering mind is futile and does real harm.
options.B: Mind wandering is chiefly productive work on plans and unfinished problems, and its costs have been exaggerated by narrowly designed experiments.
options.C: The opposed verdicts on mind wandering largely reflect the different occasions studied; its worth depends on when it occurs and whether it is noticed.
options.D: Mind wandering is better understood as a symptom of unhappiness than as its cause, contrary to what researchers at first believed.

passage: When people imagine an intelligent animal, they usually imagine something built on the plan of their own bodies: a large brain in the head that gathers information, makes decisions and issues commands to obedient limbs. The octopus is a standing challenge to that picture. Its evolutionary line separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently. And it was assembled on a strikingly different plan, for more of the octopus's neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain.

The arrangement has consequences that can be observed. An octopus arm can carry out a sequence of movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to draw it in, with little apparent direction from the centre, and an arm separated from the body will for a time continue to respond to touch and to grasp what it meets. Each arm, it seems, handles much of the detail of its own movement, while the central brain sets broader goals. Instead of a commander and its troops, the better image might be a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business.

Popular writing has been quick to turn this into a slogan, describing the octopus as an animal with nine brains, or as a colony of minds sharing one body. The slogan goes too far. The arms are not independent agents with purposes of their own; they share a body, a nervous system and, in ordinary life, a single course of action, and the animal behaves as one creature pursuing one end at a time. What the anatomy shows is not that the octopus is many minds but that one mind can be organised so that much of its work is done at the edges.

That is the real lesson, and it reaches beyond octopuses. Much thinking about intelligence, in animals and in machines alike, has assumed that it must be centralised: that there must be some single place where everything comes together and is decided. The octopus suggests that centralisation is one solution among several, suited to some bodies and not to others. An animal with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve, since each arm can bend at any point along its length and in any direction. Handing much of the work to the arms may be less an evolutionary curiosity than a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has.

options.A: the advantage to an animal that often loses arms of having limbs that can go on acting on their own.
options.B: the small size of the octopus's central brain, which leaves it unable to issue commands to its arms.
options.C: the difficulty, for any single centre, of controlling flexible and boneless limbs that can bend at any point.
options.D: the very long period during which the octopus lineage has evolved apart from vertebrates.

passage: Few technical metaphors have succeeded as completely as the cloud. To store files 'in the cloud' is to imagine them floating somewhere overhead, available from anywhere, belonging to no place in particular and weighing nothing at all. The image is not simply wrong; from the point of view of a user, it describes the experience rather well. A photograph taken on a phone appears on a laptop moments later, and the user neither knows nor needs to know where it has been in between. Yet the metaphor has migrated from describing an experience to shaping how whole societies think about a vast industrial system, and in that second role it misleads.

What sits behind the cloud is emphatically material. It consists of large buildings filled with servers, which consume great quantities of electricity and must be kept cool, often with water drawn from local supplies; of cables laid across sea floors and along railway lines; of particular sites chosen for cheap power, favourable taxes or stable ground. Each of these is somewhere, and being somewhere means being subject to the laws of a particular state, to the weather and geology of a particular region, and to the politics of the towns asked to host the buildings and supply their power. A data centre can strain a local grid or compete with farms for water, and a damaged cable can slow communication across a region.

The metaphor makes all of this hard to see. A cloud has no address, so questions about which country's courts can demand access to stored data come to seem technical rather than political. A cloud uses nothing, so the energy cost of keeping old files indefinitely available is easy to forget. And a cloud is diffuse, which suggests resilience, whereas in practice a large share of the services people rely on may depend on a small number of companies and sites, so that a single failure can ripple outward with surprising speed.

Defenders of the metaphor might point out that hiding complexity is precisely what good computing does. Nobody wants to think about the location of a server before sending a message, and abstractions of this kind are why ordinary people can use powerful systems at all. That is true, but it confuses two audiences. Abstraction is a gift to the user at the moment of use; it becomes a liability when it is carried over into the deliberations of citizens, regulators and planners, whose task is precisely to decide where the buildings go, who supplies their power and whose laws govern what they hold. For them, the useful question is not where the cloud is but how it came to seem to be nowhere.

options.A: It concedes that hiding complexity is what good computing does and therefore withdraws the earlier criticism of the metaphor.
options.B: It argues that ordinary users ought to learn where their data is physically stored before they make use of online services.
options.C: It answers a defence of the metaphor by separating what users need from what those who govern the infrastructure need.
options.D: It brings forward fresh evidence about the environmental costs of data centres to reinforce the claims of paragraph 2.

passage: A familiar answer to the question of why citizens owe obedience to their state is that they have agreed to it. Few of us, of course, ever signed anything, so the agreement is said to be tacit: by continuing to live within a country's borders, using its roads and accepting the protection of its courts, a person signals consent to its authority. The view is attractive because it seems to reconcile two things that are otherwise difficult to hold together, allowing us to say that political authority is genuinely binding while also maintaining that no one is bound against their will, since anyone who objects remains free to leave.

The trouble lies in that word 'free'. We do not normally count a choice as consent unless the person had a real alternative that could be taken at a bearable cost. Imagine a mining town with a single employer that also owns every shop, and suppose the company announces that anyone who keeps buying bread at its counters has thereby accepted all of its rules. No one would treat the purchase of bread as agreement, because the only way to refuse is to give up eating or to give up the town. Leaving a country is usually costlier still: it can mean abandoning one's language, one's family, one's work and the only place one knows well. There is, moreover, a further difficulty: almost every habitable stretch of the earth is now claimed by some state, so the emigrant does not escape political authority at all. She merely exchanges one authority for another, if another will admit her. The option on offer is not freedom from rule but the choice of a ruler.

Defenders of the view have a reasonable reply. Consent, they say, comes in degrees, and the availability of exit is not nothing. A state that lets its citizens leave, and lets them take their savings with them, really does treat them differently from one that seals its borders, and it seems right to say that the first has a stronger claim on their loyalty. This should be granted. A right of exit is a genuine good, and a state that denies it has failed one important test of legitimacy.

But to grant this is not to rescue the theory. That free exit is a condition of legitimacy does not make it the source of legitimacy, any more than an unlocked door makes a house a home. If a state's authority over those who stay can be justified, the justification must come from what the state does for and to them: whether its laws are fairly made, whether its burdens are fairly shared, whether its protection is extended to all. The language of tacit consent tends to obscure this question, since it allows a state to take credit for the mere fact that people have not fled, and to treat the absence of an escape as though it were an act of agreement.

options.A: citizens owe obedience to their state only if they have signed an explicit agreement to obey its laws and accept its courts.
options.B: tacit consent is a sound basis for political authority provided that emigration is made cheap and easy for every citizen.
options.C: the right to leave a country is the most important test of whether a state's authority over its citizens is legitimate.
options.D: merely living in a country cannot supply the consent that would legitimise its authority, though the freedom to leave still matters.

passage: The familiar story of urbanisation runs in one direction. People leave the countryside for the city, struggle for a generation in its least desirable quarters, and are eventually absorbed, their children speaking the city's idiom and regarding the village as a place of grandparents and holidays. Migration, on this account, is a passage with a beginning and an end, and the only question worth asking about a migrant is how far along it he has come. The story is not false; it describes what happened to many families in many countries. But it has acquired the status of a norm, against which other patterns are measured and found wanting, and this has made it difficult to see a pattern that is, in much of the world, at least as common.

A large number of those who work in cities never complete the journey the story describes. They come for a season of construction or a few years in a factory, return for the harvest, a wedding or an illness in the family, and come back again, sometimes to the same city and sometimes to another. Their earnings pay school fees and debts in the village; the village holds their land, their elders and, often, their spouses and children. A household can live this way for decades, and many do. Seen through the one-way story, such people are migrants who have not yet settled, a transitional population whose double life is a symptom of incomplete integration. Seen on its own terms, the pattern looks rather different: a way of spreading risk across two places, so that a lost job in the city or a failed crop in the village need not be ruinous, because the other place remains.

The distinction matters because city governments have tended to act on the first reading. A resident whose household is registered elsewhere, whose stay is irregular, and whose address is a worksite or a shared rented room is easily treated as a visitor: excluded from subsidised housing, from schools for the children who come along, from the electoral roll, and from the attention of politicians who answer to those who are on it. The exclusion then produces the very evidence that justifies it. Denied a secure foothold in the city, the circular migrant has every reason to keep the village in reserve, and the persistence of his village ties is then cited as proof that he never really belonged.

It would be a mistake to romanticise circulation in its turn. Some who move back and forth would settle in the city if they could, and return to the village only because the city offers them nothing to stay for; for them, circularity is less a strategy than a sentence. Others genuinely prefer a life lived in two places and would keep it even if the city were more welcoming. The difficulty is that from the outside the two groups look identical, and a policy designed for one will misjudge the other.

What follows is not a single programme but a change in the condition attached to belonging. A city that made its entitlements portable, that allowed a worker to enrol his children in school without proving permanent residence, and that encouraged cheap rental housing suited to stays of months rather than decades would serve both groups at once. It would allow those who wish to settle to do so, and those who wish to circulate to circulate without penalty. What it would cease to do is demand that a person surrender one home as the price of being recognised in another.

options.A: would persuade migrants who prefer a life in two places to settle permanently in the city instead.
options.B: would help both migrants forced to circulate and those who choose to, without the city having to tell the two groups apart.
options.C: would end circular migration altogether by removing the hostility of cities that is its underlying cause.
options.D: would identify which migrants wish to settle, so that each group could be offered a programme designed for it.
